description: Scenario set for the org-dysfunction loop harness. Positive scenarios test ROUTING (does the skill pull the right reference?) and TRIGGERING (should the skill fire at all?). Negative scenarios are near-misses that share vocabulary but should NOT trigger. expected_refs are reference file slugs (without .md); list every acceptable target.

scenarios.prompt: our daily standup has basically become everyone reading out what they did yesterday to the team lead, who nods and writes it down. nobody actually listens to anyone else because we're all on totally separate tickets. people keep asking if we can just kill it. is there a better format?

every retro we raise the same 3 problems (slow approvals, unclear priorities, too many deps on the platform team) and every retro we write the same action items and nothing changes. the team is getting cynical about retros entirely. what am I doing wrong as a facilitator?

leadership set the company OKRs and now each department head is 'cascading' them down to us. we're told we 'own' our team OKRs but honestly we're just rewording the VP's objectives in our own words. then we score them 0-1.0 every quarter and it feeds into reviews. feels hollow.

our CTO wants every team to hit elite DORA numbers this quarter. we built grafana dashboards for deploy freq and lead time and set targets. we got a bump for a month then it slid back and now he's asking for 'more discipline'. starting to feel like we're gaming numbers.

we did an agile transformation 18 months ago, teams supposedly have autonomy now, but decisions still take forever and just die somewhere in the middle. the middle managers are in meetings all day but nothing moves. leadership thinks they're resisting and wants to send them on a mindset course.

half my team has mentally checked out. they do exactly what's asked and not one thing more, log off at 4 on the dot. HR is calling it quiet quitting and wants me to have 'motivation conversations'. these used to be really engaged people.

my manager keeps telling us we're 'empowered to make decisions' but every time we actually decide something it gets overturned upstairs or we need three sign-offs for anything that costs money. the word empowerment is starting to feel like a joke.

we're rolling out a new operating model and the consultants keep saying 'people naturally resist change' and we need a comms plan to get buy-in. but the people pushing back are our best engineers and their objections actually seem pretty reasonable to me?

our product owner has become a total bottleneck — every decision routes through her, she writes all the stories, and if she's on holiday the team basically stalls. she's brilliant but it feels like we just recreated a project manager with a different title.

leadership wants to roll out SAFe across 12 teams with PI planning, release train engineers, the whole thing. I came from a startup where small teams just shipped and I'm worried we're about to rebuild the exact hierarchy agile was supposed to remove. am I wrong?

we've had three people go off sick with burnout this year. the company response was to offer a mindfulness app subscription and a resilience webinar. nobody's talking about the fact that we're permanently understaffed and on-call is brutal.

we just spent two years building genuinely collaborative teams and now it's annual review season — everyone gets an individual rating and ranking, stack-ranked against each other. you can already feel people starting to hoard credit again.

finance just announced individual bonus targets for next year, each person gets personal KPIs. the teams we built around shared ownership are going to get torn apart by this the second people realise their bonus depends on their own number.

every department hits its own targets — support closes tickets fast, sales smashes quota, engineering ships features — but the actual customer experience is getting worse and worse and nobody owns the end to end. how does everyone win locally while we lose overall?

we ran a psychological safety workshop because the engagement survey said people don't speak up. but two weeks later someone raised a real concern in a town hall and got visibly slapped down by a director. the workshop feels like a band-aid.

execs are convinced that dropping copilot and a bunch of AI agents into our delivery process will fix our velocity problem. but our process is a mess of handoffs and approvals — I feel like we're about to automate the chaos. how do I make that argument?

we reorganised into stream-aligned teams and platform teams straight out of Team Topologies, drew all the boxes, but nothing really changed — the same people approve the same things, authority didn't actually move anywhere. we just relabelled the org chart.

we keep telling teams to 'be autonomous and make their own calls' but when they ask what we're actually trying to achieve as a company they get three different answers from three execs. how can they self-direct toward a goal nobody can state clearly?

dev and ops here are basically at war. devs throw stuff over the wall, ops blocks releases, each side has a whole folklore about how the other is incompetent. management keeps doing 'one team' offsites that last about a week.

our best engineer just told me the only way to get promoted past senior here is to become a manager and stop coding. so all our deepest technical people are being pulled out of the work they're brilliant at. seems insane but it's the ladder.

we call ourselves a learning organisation — lunch and learns, a Udemy budget, brown bags. but honestly the way we actually build software hasn't changed in years, and the stuff people 'learn' never makes it into how we work. it's theatre.

the real decisions here never happen in the meetings. they get made in side chats and corridor conversations between a couple of senior people, and the rest of us find out after. the official governance is basically a rubber stamp.

we ran a big strategy workshop, hundreds of post-its, and the facilitators went off and came back with a gorgeous synthesis deck. but half the team quietly feels like their points got merged away or reworded, and nobody really trusts the 'outcomes' we're now supposed to act on. what went wrong and how do we run these so people actually own the result?

every couple of years HR rolls out a new role-enrichment / job-crafting programme — more variety, clearer goals, learning budgets, feedback loops. it perks people up for a few months then fades, and then we do the whole thing again under a new name. why doesn't it ever stick?

we ran a big all-hands workshop — great keynote, then really good breakout group work, everyone engaged. then we had a panel of senior leaders give feedback on what the groups produced and the whole room went cold: pointed questions, people clammed up, it ended with winners and losers instead of alignment. the facilitator was excellent so I don't get what went wrong. how do we run these so they don't collapse halfway?

our exec team meets every other week and it's basically a round-robin: engineering gives an update, then product, then finance, then people, then sales. nobody really engages with anyone else's slot. anything that spans two functions ends up getting sorted in a slack DM or by the CEO afterwards, and she's now the bottleneck for half our decisions. everyone in the room is good at their job so I can't work out why we're so useless as a group. how do we fix this?

two of my devs have turned code review into a war. every PR between them ends up with passive-aggressive comments, one gets defensive and the other piles on, and now they avoid each other in standup. the team says it's just a personality clash and we've started assigning them to different parts of the codebase so their paths don't cross. it feels like a bad answer but I don't know what else to do. thoughts?

i facilitate a lot of internal workshops and i'm getting frustrated. i do everything right — icebreaker, post-its, rotation stations, dot voting to close, an energiser when the room dips — and it all runs smoothly, but people are just... polite. present but not really in it. the outputs are fine, nobody's engaged. i keep adding new techniques to my toolkit and it doesn't move the needle. what am i doing wrong?
can you reword these three OKRs to sound a bit punchier and more inspiring for the all-hands slide? here they are: ...
what's a good Jira board column setup for a kanban team — like what statuses/swimlanes would you recommend for a 6-person team?
write me a job description for a scrum master role we're hiring for, mid-level, fintech, hybrid in Oslo.
our postgres queries on the orders table got really slow after the last release. how do I figure out which indexes are missing and optimize the performance?
my manager sent me my written performance review as a 4-page PDF. can you summarise the key points and the rating into a few bullets for me?
we've got a team offsite next month, can you suggest some fun team-building activities and an icebreaker for a group of 15?
give me a one-line definition of each stage of forming-storming-norming-performing for a glossary in our onboarding doc.

we just had a programme blow up — six months late, found out three weeks before the go-live date. i went back through the reporting and it was green every single month. then i talked to two of the engineers and they said they'd been raising the integration risk since last autumn and it kept getting reworded on the way up. the steering group is now asking who failed to escalate. i don't think that's the right question but i can't articulate why. help?

we've done everything the consultants said to close the gap between product and engineering — shared planning, engineers embedded in the product teams, a joint quarterly kickoff. two years on and it's the same: product owns the roadmap, my org owns the technical decisions, and we each defend our own budget. the only person who can actually settle a trade-off between the two is the CEO, and she's swamped. our CPO and i get on fine, so i genuinely don't know what's left to fix.

i lead a platform group of about thirty engineers and architects. i pulled a rough tally of where last quarter went and it's grim — timesheet coding against eleven project codes, a monthly portfolio board, a design authority forum, a change advisory board, plus writing up decisions we'd already taken so they'd be on record for audit. actual design and build was maybe a third of the time. we've been through two efficiency programmes that both merged some forums and simplified the templates, and within a couple of quarters the load was back where it started. leadership is now asking us to justify headcount using the same reporting that's eating the capacity. i'm out of ideas that aren't just another process improvement.

my team knows exactly what we want to do with our own deployment pipeline. we've analysed it, we agree, it's our system. and yet last week we still put it on the steering group agenda 'to be safe'. nobody up there knows this system better than us. why do we keep doing this?

one on one my designers are full of opinions, but in our planning workshops they all clam up and wait for whatever the department head hints at. then they complain in the corridor afterwards. how do i get real participation in the room?

our new agile coach says the friction in my newly formed team is 'just storming' and we have to let it run its course before they can perform. it's been four months and it's getting worse, not better. is storming actually a required phase?

we're replacing a 15-year-old case management system and the team refuses to ship anything until they've mapped every behaviour of the old one. the goal has quietly become 'do exactly what the old system did'. we're eight months in with nothing live.

we told the team they're self-organising but they also have a formal team lead with delivery responsibility. now nobody knows if 'the team decided' or 'Kim approved it', and it changes depending on who you ask. the lead does servant leadership stuff but everyone still watches their face before committing to anything.

i facilitated a really carefully designed workshop yesterday — good exercises, timeboxes, materials. it fell completely flat. people did the exercises politely and left. the boss was in the room and honestly the conclusion had kind of been decided already. why don't these sessions ever produce anything?

every retro ends with 'we have a communication problem'. handoffs get missed, people are out of the loop, stuff arrives late. HR's answer is another round of communication training and a comms plan. we've done three of those. it never changes anything.

our scrum team runs beautifully — clean board, stable velocity, tidy backlog. but it feels like we're in a bubble. the rest of the org is on fire around us and none of it touches our curated backlog. is a perfectly protected team actually a good sign?

we work harder every year and respond slower. by the time our annual plan is approved the market's moved. every decision queues at the top. a competitor shipped in the time it took us to schedule the decision meeting about whether to start.

we've had three people burn out or leave from the same coordinator role in two years. each time we did a PIP or coaching for the person. the next one struggles the same way. at what point is it not about the individuals?

same categories of production errors keep recurring. after each incident we add a checklist item, a sign-off, or a training module. we now have 40-step release checklists and the error rate hasn't moved. leadership thinks people are just sloppy.

we've invested enormously in leadership development — programmes, 360s, coaching for every manager. the managers are genuinely good people. teams still underperform, engagement is mediocre, and the response to every dip is another leadership framework. what are we missing?

we dot-voted the new team structure in a big workshop and moved on — felt very democratic. but the group that lost the vote has been dragging their feet ever since and the decision needs constant chasing. did we actually decide anything?

we ran a genuinely great co-design week with the teams — eventstorming, real energy. then the architecture group reworked everything behind closed doors and the target picture that came out looks nothing like what we built together. the teams noticed. trust took a visible hit.

we paid for an external review of our architecture. the report landed and my engineers' first move was to explain why every finding 'misses our context'. the only findings they accept are the ones they already knew. was the review a waste?

we're fighting about return-to-office. leadership says collaboration needs proximity, people say they're more productive at home. but honestly, when everyone IS in the office they sit with headphones on metres apart working alone anyway. are we arguing about the wrong thing?

two of our teams were told to build the new intake flow 'together'. it started friendly. three months later one team is effectively setting all the terms and the other has gone quiet and just complies. credit lands unevenly. nobody planned this.

my engineers make product decisions all day and not one of them has ever talked to an actual user. everything arrives pre-digested — personas from UX, requirements from the PO, dashboards from analytics. they know ABOUT the customer, they've just never met one.

our director sends non-urgent mail on sunday nights with 'no need to reply before monday' in the footer. everyone replies within the hour anyway. the people getting promoted are noticeably the always-on ones. the stated policy says work-life balance.

leadership brought in a consultancy to write our three-year strategy. six months of interviews and offsites, beautiful deck, full authority. implementation died in the first quarter on questions the deck never anticipated. the people who have to execute it don't recognise the company in it.

our improvement engine is world class — efficiency programmes, restructures, all our internal KPIs trend up. meanwhile frontline people keep flagging a tech shift our roadmap ignores, and their signals die somewhere in middle management. we're getting better and better at the wrong thing.

we 'went product' last year — squads, sprints, demos. but every squad has locked scope and a hard deadline agreed above them. halfway in, a team discovered the problem is different than assumed, and the answer was 'deliver what was committed anyway'. so what exactly is product about this?

our pilot team for the new operating model was a huge success — engaged people, faster delivery, the works. the moment we proposed scaling it, resistance appeared everywhere: the other managers, HR, the architects. now the pilot is quietly sliding back to the old ways. why does this always happen to pilots?

our company champions responsible AI publicly and i think we mean it. but when someone asked at a panel about the actual environmental footprint of our AI stack, we couldn't answer — the vendor NDA literally prevents the people who know from saying. how do we square that with our sustainability commitments?

we do scrum absolutely by the book — every ceremony, on time, well run. we got a real improvement bump the first year, then plateaued, and now the same problems resurface quarterly wearing new labels. standups are status reports again. do we need a better process or is process not the lever?

our distributed team's tickets and ceremonies all run fine, but five-minute decisions take three days, small misunderstandings snowball, and we only found out a teammate was struggling when it blew up. the formal machinery works. something else doesn't.

from the outside my team looks great. inside, every real decision happens in a slack thread between the same two people. their PRs sail through, everyone else's wait. the other five engineers have become spectators. it's stable, but is it healthy?

we restructured into autonomous product teams — own roadmaps, own ways of working. then finance handed them the same centralised annual budget process: forecast 18 months out, write business cases to justify your existence, compete for a fixed pot. mid-year the money gets moved around over their heads. autonomy, but.

we set up self-managing teams eighteen months ago. performance lifted, then quietly slid back to old habits — nobody decided to roll back, it just happened. the teams keep colliding with HR's individual performance reviews and finance's project codes. the org chart says one thing, the machinery says another.

we have an advisory board, conference keynotes, seats in two industry working groups. looking honestly at it: the board reviews features we already decided, the talks describe what we already built, the working-group papers never get implemented. we look like market shapers. are we?

our strategy talks about five-year capability building. every actual decision optimises the next quarter — capability investment deferred, tech debt piling up, people restructured instead of developed because development pays off on a timescale nobody's bonus measures. how do we break the loop?

something i can't say out loud at work: the process is basically decoration. a platform request through the official intake sat for six weeks; a colleague mentioned it over coffee to someone who reports to the CTO and it was resourced in two days. the people who thrive here are the ones who work those channels. i'm not good at it and i'm starting to think i'm just not cut out for this place. is this a me problem?

watched our CTO approve a two-year platform migration last week. the team had spent months on the evaluation — a proper comparison doc, every dimension covered. he got a fifteen-minute readout and signed. afterwards someone asked him in the corridor why we picked that vendor and he genuinely couldn't say. now he owns the outcome and the four people who actually understand the trade-offs own nothing. it feels absurd but i can't tell if i'm being unfair to him.

we did a two-day offsite with an external facilitator last spring and came out with five values — courage, trust, impact, collaboration, excellence. they're on the wall in reception and on every slide template. i asked three people in my team last week to name them and none of them could get past two. leadership is now planning a 'values relaunch' campaign with posters and a video. i think the words are fine, honestly, but something about the whole thing feels fake and i can't articulate why. am i just being cynical?

we were about three weeks behind on a delivery so our manager brought in a contractor. we found out at monday standup when she introduced him. he's competent but he needed environments, access, domain context, someone to pair with — and all of that came out of the two people who were already the bottleneck. a month later we're further behind than when he started and nobody wants to say it out loud because it sounds like we're blaming him. was this always going to happen?

we had a payment outage last night and honestly the team was incredible - four of us on a call, found the cause, shipped the fix, done in about 90 minutes, nobody asked permission for anything. now the same engineer wants to make the proper permanent fix and it's been sitting in a change-approval queue for three days. people keep joking that we should just declare an incident whenever we want to get something done. how do I make the argument that the incident way of working should be the normal way?

i'm in a setup where i report to an engineering manager for my discipline and to a product owner for delivery. last week my eng manager signed me up for a two-day course starting thursday and the same afternoon my PO told the stakeholders the feature ships friday. neither of them talked to each other about it, and both of them are right in their own way. i ended up doing the course badly and the feature badly. this happens maybe once a month and it always lands on me to pick. HR calls it a matrix organisation. how do i stop being the person who has to choose?

we ran an all-day session with about 20 people from across the department. to get through everything we split into four groups of five, each took one of the big questions, and after 90 minutes every group presented back a summary. it felt really productive on the day. but now a week later i'm finding people only remember whatever their own group discussed - they can't tell me what the other three decided, and two of the decisions are already being argued about again by people who weren't at that table. was our report-back too rushed? should i have written a better summary document afterwards?

we spent two years reorganising into cross-functional product teams and honestly internally it's night and day - the teams decide things themselves now and ship weekly. but everything that touches our platform vendor has gotten worse, or at least it feels worse now by comparison. a config change we need is item 140-something on their global roadmap and their product council reviews it quarterly. their support is three tiers of tickets so when our engineer knows exactly which of their engineers could fix it in ten minutes, there is no way for those two to speak. our account manager is lovely and completely powerless. i'm getting asked whether we should put them on a performance improvement plan or find a tougher procurement lead. is that the answer?

our ceo read reinventing organizations two years ago and we went all in on teal. titles became roles, we brought in the advice process instead of sign-off chains, there's a whole page on the wiki about the colours and everyone can talk about it fluently. two of the eight teams are genuinely flying. the rest quietly still ask their old line manager before doing anything, and the managers themselves are the ones pushing back hardest so we've stopped rolling it out any further. our coach keeps telling us the organisation isn't ready yet and needs more inner work before the next wave, and we've now booked another round of consciousness workshops. i'm starting to wonder if we're just not evolved enough as a group, or whether we picked the wrong people to start with?

we just got an email saying everyone is back in the office five days a week from next month. the reasons given were collaboration, culture and mentoring the juniors. we've been remote for three years and honestly the numbers haven't moved either way — the teams that worked well still work well, the ones that struggled still struggle, and nobody has pointed at anything specific that was failing. half the meetings that got moved back into a room have people dialling in anyway. i'm a team lead and my people are asking me to justify it. how do i think about this?

we're a fairly green company, iso certified on the environmental side, we publish our own green coding standards and we track component reuse. last quarter we rolled out ai coding assistants to all twelve dev teams and it's gone well, people like them. what's been nagging me is that nobody anywhere is measuring what all that inference actually costs in compute or emissions. the green coding standards were written in 2023 and don't mention ai at all so technically nothing is being breached. i asked around about who owns figuring out the impact and got shrugs — sustainability says it's an engineering tooling decision, engineering says sustainability sets the standards. the only thing we seem to produce on this is the annual disclosure. am i wrong to think this is a real gap, and who should i be pushing?

we lost someone in march who i now realise was holding the whole team together. she wasn't a manager, she was a senior dev, but she onboarded every new person, kept our docs actually current, and somehow always caught the friction between two of the guys before it turned into anything. none of that was in her objectives. since she left, onboarding has stalled, two people are barely speaking, and stuff keeps falling between us that used to just get handled. management's answer is that we clearly need a dedicated team lead and they're recruiting externally for a coordinator. my gut says that's not going to work — the new person won't know the domain or any of us — but i can't articulate why beyond a feeling. how should i be thinking about this?

our leadership rolled out what they call a tight-loose-tight model about a year ago. the idea is they set the direction, we decide how to get there, and then they check the outcome. on paper i liked it. in practice my team keeps discovering walls we didn't know were there — we picked a queue technology and were told to use the standard one, we resequenced two deliverables and that got reversed, we wanted to cut a feature we're pretty sure nobody wants and were told the scope was already committed. nobody can give me a list of what we actually get to decide. the targets come down from the portfolio review and the same review decides whether we hit them. my team has basically stopped proposing anything, and now i'm getting feedback that they seem to lack ownership. what's actually going on here?

i'm running a two-day workshop next month on how work flows end to end across our delivery org — the handoffs between product, dev, test and ops are where everything gets stuck and we want to redesign it properly. my sponsor and i built the invite list last week: the three department directors, our two principal engineers, someone senior from IT operations, the four project managers, and an enterprise architect. twenty people, everyone with real authority to make decisions stick. i've booked a good facilitator and we've got a solid agenda. one of my team asked why none of the people who actually run the handoffs day to day are on the list and i brushed it off — we can't fit everyone and these are the people who can actually change things. now it's nagging at me. is there something wrong with how i've composed this room?

we rolled out a whole mental health package about eight months ago — EAP contract, headspace licences for everyone, mindfulness sessions in the big meeting room at lunch on tuesdays, posters in the kitchen about checking in on each other. our CPO talks about work-life balance at every all-hands and we introduced a policy discouraging emails after 6pm. HR is pleased, sign-up on the app is something like 70% and the sessions are well attended. the problem is stress-related sick leave is exactly where it was. flat. same absolute numbers, roughly the same people. i had to present the wellbeing update to the leadership team last week and someone asked whether any of this is actually doing anything, and honestly i don't have an answer. the suggestion on the table now is to invest more in promotion and add resilience training. i'm not convinced but i can't articulate why.

something is bothering me about how our AI rollout has gone and i can't quite name it. we gave the whole engineering org copilot-style assistants about a year ago and the delivery numbers are genuinely up, leadership is delighted. but our developers barely design anything now. they write a prompt, skim the diff, ship it. i used to have people who could hold a whole subsystem in their head and argue with me about the shape of it, and those arguments were where the good decisions came from. now the shape just arrives and nobody pushes back. the juniors we hired this year have never done it any other way. when i raised it with my director he said this is just what modern engineering looks like and i'm being nostalgic, and that if people feel left behind they should upskill. i don't think that's the whole story but i can't argue it properly. is this the tool's fault or ours?

we paid for a proper target operating model last year. our enterprise architect did the work and honestly it was good — every capability mapped, clean domain boundaries, the interfaces between them all specified, owners named. the exec team signed it off and everyone agreed it described us accurately. eighteen months on it describes almost nothing. teams have quietly routed around half the boundaries, the handoffs that matter go the wrong way across the interfaces, and when i raise it in the architecture forum the framing is always that the teams have drifted out of compliance and we need tighter governance to pull them back. nobody has suggested the model might be the thing that's wrong. i can't shake the feeling something was missing from it on day one and i still can't name what.

we took out our entire middle management layer in january — partly cost, mostly because leadership wanted us to be flatter and faster. teams were told they're self-managing now. six months in and things are slower, not faster. all the stuff those managers did is still there: someone has to decide what we do first when three stakeholders all want something, someone has to go chase the thing stuck in another department, someone has to hold the context. in practice one person on each team has ended up doing it, with no title and no real authority, and if you disagree with them there's no process for that. our director's read is that the teams just aren't mature enough for autonomy yet and we should give it time. i think something else is going on but i'm struggling to argue it.
